     REPLY OF INTERVENOR JASON A. HOWTON TO EXCEPTIONS TO THE
                      PROPOSAL FOR DECISION

       Intervenor Jason A. Howton, appearing pro se, respectfully and timely files this Reply to

the Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision filed in this docket on September 2,2026, and would

respectfully show as follows:


I. INTRODUCTION
       This reply follows the outline of the Proposal for Decision as Item No. 6442 directs, and

replies only to exceptions filed on September 2,2026. It does not repeat Mr. Howton's Exceptions

(Item No. 6456), which are incorporated by reference, and it raises no new ground.

       Mr. Howton replies principally to the Exceptions of Applicants (Item No. 6484) and of

Commission Staff (Item No. 6471), which are the only filings that ask the Commission to reject

the Administrative Law Judges' recommendation of denial on both notice and need. He replies

more briefly to Delaware Basin Midstream (Item No. 6481) on need; to Save the Lampasas (Item

No. 6486) and the Link N3 Landowners (Item No. 6485) on the alternative they call Route 296


SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349; PUC Docket No. 59475                                       Page 4
Howton' s Reply to Exceptions
 Option A; to the Link Rl Landowners (Item No. 6464), Mr. Sneed (Item No. 6483), Carpenter

Land and Cattle (Item No. 6476), the M31/M32/M33 Landowners (Item No. 6474), the J27/J25/J4

Landowners (Item No. 6465), and Yates (Item No. 6455) on routes that retain Links F20 and F23;

and to the parties who object to Route 296.

       Mr. Howton's objection is to Links F20 and F23. He takes no position against any route

that avoids both. The link-level record that follows supports that route-level position; it is offered

because a route-level objection to Route 894 has to rest on something more specific than the route's

name, not as a request for link-by-link relief independent of the route the Commission ultimately

considers.

       Three things stand out from the thirty-four exceptions filed.

       First, no party has filed a record-based argument that Links F20 and F23 are preferable to

the alternative Applicants themselves carried into the Application in Route 899. Applicants' eighty

pages contain no routing section and do not mention either link. Staff recommends Route 487,

which carries both links, without mentioning either. Every other filing that retains the two links

does so as part of a western-half alternative to Route 894 and says nothing about Bell County.

Additional Section A sets out the census.

        Second, Applicants ask the Commission to approve the Project "along any ofthe alternative

routes included for consideration in the applications," and their Replacement Conclusion of Law

14 reads: "The transmission facilities using route      are necessary. Ill

       After a hearing, two rounds of briefs, and a round of exceptions, the Applicants have not

asked the Commission to find that Route 894 is the route.




   1 Applicants' Exceptions at 5, 34 (Item No. 6484)
SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349; PUC Docket No. 59475                                             Page 5
Howton' s Reply to Exceptions
          Third, Applicants and Staff argue that Docket No. 59315 settled the public-meeting

question. But that memorandum did not answer the limiting principle presented by this record.

Approximately 2,800 landowners were within the affected class when Applicants held the June

2025 meetings. Afterward, Applicants expanded the routing by roughly 400 miles, so that

approximately 4,200 landowners were within the class entitled to application notice when the CCN

was filed. Roughly 1,400 Texans therefore received application notice without ever receiving the

same pre-application meeting notice afforded to the earlier group. Chairman Gleeson's

memorandum described compliance by reference to the project "as it existed at the time."2

         Separately, under subsection (a)(3), Findings of Fact 40 through 42 find that over three

dozen directly affected landowners were not noticed on the filing date and that five were noticed

sixty-seven days later, after the April 27,2026 intervention deadline had passed. Applicants' own

Replacement Finding of Fact 39 concedes the late notice. That separate application-notice defect

compounds the public-meeting problem; it does not create the subsection (a)(4) violation. 3


V. PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUES 1-4

B. Notice

         Staff makes the same request on the ground that " [ilt is not explicitly clear what 'current

county tax rolls' means.   Il 5




        a. The dates are not disputed, and the late notice is conceded. Neither Applicants nor

Staff disputes Finding of Fact 3 9, which records that the appraisal-district data used for the March

26,2026 notices was pulled between December 8,2025 and February 23,2026, or Finding ofFact

42, which names the landowners noticed on May 26 and June 1, 2026. Applicants' Replacement

Finding of Fact 39 states that "[alfter the Application was filed, Applicants identified additional

landowners who had not received direct-mail notice of the Application" and that Applicants

"provided supplemental notice."6

        Their Replacement Finding of Fact 40 concedes that of the forty-two landowners so

noticed, twenty are directly affected within the meaning of the rule.7

        The dispute is therefore not whether directly affected landowners were noticed after the

intervention deadline. It is whether that is a violation. The rule requires notice "on the date it files

an application. 118

        Notice sixty-seven days later to a landowner whose intervention deadline was April 27,

2026 is not notice on the date of filing under any reading of"current."

        b. Stall's textual argument proves the opposite. Staff argues that "on the date it files an

application" modifies "mail" and that nothing links "current" to the filing date.9

        That reading concedes that the mailing must occur on the filing date. A mailing on the

filing date to a roll that is three months stale does not reach the persons who are "directly affected"

 on the filing date, and the rule's purpose is to reach them. Staffs construction would permit a utility

to pull rolls a year early, mail on the filing date, and satisfy the rule while the actual owners receive

nothing. "Current" has to mean something, and the only date the rule supplies is the filing date.

                c. Project No. 58400 declined a different benchmark, and the reason the Commission

gave runs against Applicants. Applicants' principal argument is that in Project No. 58400 the

Office ofPublic Utility Counsel asked the Commission to amend Rule 22.52(a)(3) to mirror Texas

Water Code § 13.246(a-1) by tying the tax-roll data to the time the Commission receives the

application, and that the Commission declined. That is accurate, and Mr. Howton does not contend

that the rule requires the rolls to be downloaded on the filing date.10

                Applicants then quote the reason the Commission gave, and the reason answers the

argument. The Commission declined the change as "unnecessary" because "the rule provision as

proposed entitles directly affected landowners to notice, which more accurately identifies persons

with a justiciable interest compared to those landowners on the county tax rolls as of a particular

date.   II 11




                The Commission refused to substitute a dated list for a class-based entitlement because the

entitlement is the more protective of the two. It runs to the persons who are directly affected,

whoever they are on the filing date. Applicants' own Replacement Finding of Fact 40 concedes

that twenty of the landowners first noticed on May 26 and June 1, 2026 are directly affected within

the meaning ofthe rule. Project No. 58400 identifies who is entitled to notice. It does not hold that

the entitlement may go unmet.

         The same passage says the Commission was "not aware of any issues with the current

notice process that warrants such a revision." That order issued on February 5,2026, seven weeks

before this Application was filed and four months before the notice record in this docket was

developed. A statement that the Commission knew of no problem with the process is not a ruling

that what happened here complied with it.

        d. Docket No. 55768 addresses county-record lag, not applicant-data lag. As

Applicants describe that case, CenterPoint consulted county tax-roll data roughly three months

before filing, and the county records themselves had not yet reflected certain new ownership; the

Commission found that gap reasonable. 12

        A record source lagging behind reality is not the defect here. The Proposal for Decision's

finding concerns staggered snapshots Applicants themselves collected from December 8,2025

through February 23, 2026 and used on March 26, 2026, after which Applicants identified

additional directly affected owners the snapshots had missed. Docket No. 55768 excused a gap

between the source and the world; it did not excuse a gap between the data an applicant collected

and the data an applicant used.

        e. Rule 22.52(a)(3)(F) does not erase a front-end notice-list defect. Applicants argue

that the Proposal for Decision reads the cure provision as "a nullity." The provision states that once

proof of notice is filed, "the lack of actual notice to any individual landowner will not in and of

itself support a finding that the requirements of this paragraph have not been satisfied. Il 13

        The operative words are "in and of itself." The provision answers the case of individual

non-receipt standing alone. The Proposal for Decision did not rest on individual non-receipt

          The memorandum also observed: "Regarding notice of the application, the ALJs did find

that Oncor was compliant. " 18

         The later application notice described in Docket No. 59315 did not supply the pre-

application opportunity subsection (a)(4) protects. In this docket, the separate application-notice

failure found by the Administrative Law Judges compounds the problem; it does not create the

subsection (a)(4) violation. 19 Section V.B.2 addresses the independent public-meeting violation.

         h. The remedy argument does not reach Conclusion of Law 15. Applicants argue that

"[ tlhe remedy for a denial ofdue process is due process ," citing University of Texas Medical School

v. Than, 901 S.W.2d 926, 933 (Tex. 1995), and that the rule "prescribes a day-for-day extension

of deadlines as the remedy for deficient notice. 1120

         Three replies.

         First, the argument is made under subsection (a)(3) only. Applicants have already told this

tribunal that the day-for-day extension in Rule 22.52(a)(5) "applies to failures to comply with the

notice requirements for filing an application as set forth in 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(1)-(3)" and that

"[nlothing in the text ofthe rule extends the day-for-day extension remedy to the public meeting

context. ll21

         Conclusion of Law 15 rests on subsection (a)(4). On Applicants' own construction,

subsection (a)(5) never supplied a remedy for that violation, and the Administrative Law Judges'

conclusion that no lesser remedy remains is compelled by Applicants' own reading. 22

         Second , Than does not hold what Applicants cite it for . The Court there vacated the
dismissal and remanded so that the student could receive the process he had been denied; it did not

award the university the benefit of the proceeding it had conducted without him. 23

        The Proposal for Decision's remedy, denial without prejudice to an application filed on

compliant notice, is Than's remedy: the process the rule requires, provided to the persons the rule

protects, before the decision is made. Applicants' proposed remedy, additional process without

denial, does not explain how the pre-application process the rule required can be supplied after the

Application has been filed and the merits hearing completed , which is the problem Than addresses .

        Third, the extension Applicants describe is one they have told the Commission it cannot

grant. In Docket No. 59315 Oncor argued that PURA § 37.057 admits "no 'good cause' exception,

no tolling mechanism, and no provision authorizing the Commission or SOAH to suspend or

continue the 180-day period.„24

        A remedy that extends "deadlines for intervention and for commission action" cannot

operate where, on the utility's own account, the second deadline cannot be extended and the first

has passed. That is why the Administrative Law Judges concluded the remedy "is no longer

available here. 1125

        i. On "delay or distract." Applicants write that the notice challenges "are driven primarily

by Intervenors Kevin Kennedy and John Burrow ... whose objections serve only to delay or

distract," and point to "over 2,200 interventions" as proofthat notice worked.26

who were entitled to be told and were not. The rule protects the second group, and the

Administrative Law Judges identified them by name.

          Requested disposition. Deny Applicants' and Staff' s exceptions to Findings of Fact 38

through 43 and Conclusion of Law 10. If the Commission changes any of those findings, Rule

22.262(b) and Texas Government Code § 2003.049(h) require it to "state in writing the specific

reason and legal basis" for the change; a finding that Applicants' notice was compliant cannot rest

on a memorandum's characterization when Applicants' own replacement findings concede the late

notice.


2. Notice ofthe Public Meeting: Rule 22.52(a)(4) (Findings ofFact 22-30; Conclusions ofLaw
11 and 15)
          Reply to Applicants' Exceptions at 41-54 and Stairs Exceptions at 7-10.

          Applicants ask that Findings of Fact 22 through 30 and Conclusions of Law 11 and 15 be

deleted and replaced with a single finding and a single conclusion. 27

          Staff asks that Finding ofFact 30 and Conclusion ofLaw 11 be deleted.28

          a. No party contests Findings of Fact 22 through 29 as facts. Neither filing disputes that

Applicants expanded the study area after the June 2025 meetings, added roughly 400 miles of

links, and brought approximately 1,400 additional landowners within the class entitled to

application notice without holding a further meeting. Staff quotes the 1,400 figure from the

Proposal for Decision in its own footnote.29

              Applicants' Replacement Finding ofFact 22 says only that Kimley-Horn and Halff "made

several modifications to the preliminary route segments. 1130

             "Several modifications" is not a finding that contradicts Findings ofFact 22 through 29; it

is a finding that omits them. The Environmental Assessment records fifty-odd added links and

states that the expansion was made because "Oncor and LCRA TSC asked Kimley-Horn and Halff

to evaluate and consider expansion of the breadth of alternative route links throughout the study

area. ll31
             The expansion was Applicants' request, not a response to public comment. These findings

are supported by the record and by the silence of every party, and Texas Government Code §

2001.141(c) provides that "[f]indings of fact may be based only on the evidence and on matters

that are officially noticed." A finding cannot be struck "to accurately reflect the evidentiary record"

when the record is what it reflects.

             b. Applicants' statement of the rule adds words to it. Applicants restate the rule as

requiring "direct-mail notice ofthat meeting to owners within 500 feet ... of the centerline of the

transmission project as it exists at the time ofthe public meeting. 1132

             The phrase "as it exists at the time of the public meeting" is not in 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4).

The rule's trigger is "if 25 or more persons would be entitled to receive direct mail notice of the

application ." Applicants then invoke Laidlaw Waste Systems, Inc. v. Wilmer , 904 S . W . 2d 656 , 659

(Tex. 1995), for the proposition that "every word excluded from a statute must also be presumed

to have been excluded for a purpose. 1133

         That is Mr. Howton's point. The words on which Applicants' reading depends are the words

the Commission excluded. Port Arthur Communio, Action Network v. TCEQ, 707 S.W.3d 102,

104 (Tex. 2025), which Applicants also cite, requires that a rule be applied "based first and

foremost on a natural reading oftheir plain text. 1134

        The clear text ties the meeting to the class entitled to notice of the application, and that

class is fixed on the filing date by subsection (a)(3), not on the meeting date. The next sentence

points the same way: it requires meeting notice to owners within 500 feet of the centerline of "a

transmission project" greater than 230 kV. Read together with the first sentence and the

Commission's adoption-order statement discussed below that public-meeting notice would

"mirror" CCN application notice, the text does not support freezing the meeting-notice population

to whatever preliminary links happened to exist on the date Applicants chose to hold the meetings.

        Applicants have said so themselves. In this docket they wrote that " [tlhe rule mandates a

public meeting only if 25 or more persons would be entitled to receive direct mail notice. 1135

        The measuring class, in Applicants' words, is the class entitled to notice of the application.

Here that class was approximately 4,200 owners on the filing date and approximately 2,800 when

the meetings were held. 36

        c. The construction has a stopping point; Applicants' does not. Applicants argue that

the Administrative Law Judges' reading would require "a potentially endless cycle ofmeetings. 1137

        It would not. The trigger is numerical, and it supplies the limit: a further meeting is owed

when the persons newly entitled to notice ofthe application themselves satisfy the rule's threshold

 oftwenty-five. Here roughly 1,400 owners were newly brought within it, more than fifty times the

rule's own figure. The Administrative Law Judges in Docket No. 59315 stated the same limit:


        "If by the filing ofthe application, it is determined that there are 25 or more owners
        of directly affected land, the utility is subject to the public meeting requirement and
        must notice and convene that meeting prior to filing its application. It matters not
        that at some earlier point during the routing study there were fewer than 25 owners

        It is Applicants' reading that has no stopping point. Under it, the persons entitled to meeting

notice are fixed on the day of the meeting, and nothing the utility does afterward, whether moving

the centerline two thousand feet, adding four hundred miles of links, or relocating the corridor into

a neighboring county inside the study area, requires a meeting, meeting notice, or newspaper notice

until the application is filed. Applicants confirm this is their position: "the rule imposes no

obligation to hold a public meeting for landowners identified only after the single required meeting

has already occurred. 1139

        When the Commission adopted the meeting requirement, AEP objected that "at the time of

the public meeting numerous preliminary routes are still under consideration," and the

Commission answered by limiting meeting notice "to correspond to the two-tier notice requirement

applicable to landowners," concluding: "Therefore, the notice for public meetings will mirror the

direct mail notice required for CCN applications. 1140

        The Commission heard the argument that preliminary routes change, and answered it by

tying the meeting class to the application class. A reading under which the two classes may diverge

by 1,400 persons does not mirror anything.
